claims.claim: The legate Morone's party reached Augsburg on the eve of the Annunciation (24 March 1555)
The King of the Romans, the Cardinal of Augsburg and other bishops and princes received them and came out almost a league to meet the legate
Word that Julius was dying reached Augsburg on the 27th, and news of his death on the 29th (the file reads 'Julius II', sic)
Morone left for Rome on the last day of March, with the Cardinal of Augsburg
Sarpi says Julius died as soon as Morone arrived, and that Morone had word of it 'eight days after'
Julius III died on 23 March 1555
Polanco is the secretary of the Society of Jesus, writing its chronicle for 1555

Julius III sent Morone only 'con ripugnanza estrema' (OCR 'edrema'), since religion was to be handled in an assembly mixed of churchmen and laymen, Catholics and heretics; 'alla qual mostruosità non pareua conueneuole spettatore vn Legato' (OCR 'moftruofità', 'conue-|neuolc fpettatore')
Pallavicino was a Jesuit ('della Compagnia di Gesù'); the held edition is his revised one of 1664, the first having appeared in 1656-1657
Pallavicino's history was written to refute Sarpi's ('un'istoria falsa ... sotto nome di Pietro Soave Polano')
Sarpi was a Venetian friar ('Father Paul the Venetian, of the Order'; 'Fryer Paul')
This Diet met in 1555, twenty-five years after the Augsburg Confession was read at the Diet of 1530; the recess protects that confession without naming a year or edition
Sarpi says the emperor 'had intimated' the Diet 'principally to compose the Controversies of Religion', which was 'the Fountain of all the troubles, and calamities of Germany' (long s normalized)
Sarpi says Ferdinand began the Diet in the emperor's name on 5 February
The Monumenta editors say the Augsburg assembly of 1555 began on 5 February and closed in September
Ferdinand's opening, in Sarpi: a general, free and pious council was once thought the only remedy; why it bore no fruit was known to all; a national council was out of use
Ferdinand, in Sarpi: colloquies did no good because both parties aimed at private gain; yet he counselled trying one once more if the Diet did not propose a better way
The proposal also concerned peace and war with the Turks, and was meant to invite men to the Diet, 'to which very few were come'
The recess says the peace was made 'der spaltigen religion halben' as the high need of the empire required
The recess says the peace was granted to save 'diese lobliche nation vor endlichem vorsteendem undergang' (OCR 'lobhche')
Julius III's two conditions: great lords in person, not proxies; and nothing settled against the authority of the Church, the Fathers and the councils, above all against Trent's decisions
Sarpi says the legate was instructed 'above all, to divert all Colloquies, and Treaties of Religion'
Sarpi says Julius cursed the colloquies and their inventors, and complained he would always have 'a Council, a Colloquy, or a Diet' on his back
Polanco reports Canisius: all Catholics thought it would have been far wiser never to have begun the Diet, and feared its end would be a great harm to faith and church jurisdiction
Sarpi says those of the Augsburg Confession claimed it was lawful for all to accept their doctrine, keeping the honors, states and offices they held (OCR has lost part of 'Offices')

Ferdinand's defence, in Pallavicino: the Protestant princes of Saxony, Brandenburg and Hesse met at Naumburg 'quasi in vna Contradieta' (OCR 'vua') and wrote to Ferdinand of confirming their hereditary league
The 1648 treaty names 'Transactio a. 1552 Passavii inita et hanc a. 1555 secuta pax religionis'
Pallavicino's article: seizures of church goods were left to the Concord of Passau and suspended until a future diet
Charles V called the Diet; Ferdinand opened it 'in the Emperours name'
Ferdinand's defence, in Pallavicino: Charles answered 'in secca forma' that sickness and war kept him from German affairs, 'Onde à esso Ferdinando ne rimettea la dispositione'
Ferdinand was Charles's brother: Pallavicino has the emperor and 'il Rè suo fratello' (OCR 'lùo'); Sarpi's 'Imperial Authority of his Brother' reads 'of - us Brother' in the OCR
The recess speaks as 'we' beside 'der Röm. Kai. Mt' (OCR 'Köm.'); Mirbt's extract does not name the speaker
Polanco places the King of the Romans at Augsburg ('qui tunc Augustae agebat')
Salmerón had an audience with the King of the Romans at Augsburg, reported in his letter of 1 September 1555
Nadal was sent with the legate Morone to the Diet of Augsburg in February 1555, and Lainez joined them at Florence

claims.claim: Lainez left Augsburg on 2 April
Nadal wrote from Augsburg on 30 March, 6 April and 17 April 1555

claims.claim: The Cardinal of Augsburg is Otto Truchsess, by the Monumenta editors' note
Pallavicino: the nuncio Delfino, on Paul IV's election, asked for a successor and was told to commend his business to Luigi Lippomano, bishop of Verona, who was going as nuncio to Poland

Lippomano gave Ferdinand 'vna ponderosa scrittura' (OCR 'pende rofa_» fcrittufa') arguing questions of faith have no tribunal but the Apostolic See, then went on to Poland rather than stay a 'spettatore poco onorato'
Salmerón, of the party of the nuncio of Verona (Lippomano) for Poland, reached Augsburg on 20 August 1555, where the nuncio received them
The Monumenta editors say Salmerón's party left Augsburg on 7 September
Canisius was at Augsburg most of June (after the 9th) and from the last days of July to 5 August, by the editors' dating after Braunsberger
Canisius preached twice at Augsburg and blocked a public disputation that seemed full of danger
Nadal and Lainez met the bishop of Laibach and Pedro de Soto, 'olim Imperatoris Caroli confessario'; Soto left the Diet called by Philip, king of England
The 1648 treaty says the 1555 peace was made with the unanimous consent of the emperor, electors, princes and estates of both religions
Ferdinand's defence in Pallavicino: he had only approved what 'Cattolici ed Eretici, Ecclesiastici e Secolari' had agreed together (OCR 'vintamente', 'Ecclefiaftici')
The recess is dated 25 September 1555
claims.witness: mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.16247-16248; sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.38443-38444; polanco_chronicon-v5-lat_1897.txt l.2509, 2542-2545 (the editors quoting Braunsberger)

claims.claim: Pallavicino says the recess came out 'in sù lo spirar di Settembre'
Paul IV's two letters are dated 18 December 1555
Paul IV was elected on 23 May 1555
§15: no estate of the empire to be attacked, harmed or forced on account of the Augsburg Confession 'wider sein conscienz, gewissen und willen'
§15: the protection covers the religion and order set up or to be set up 'in iren fürstentumben, lan-|den und herschaften', with goods and lordships
§15: the disputed religion to be brought to agreement only 'durch christliche, freuntlihe [sic OCR], friedliche mittel und wege'
§16: the estates of the Augsburg Confession to leave the estates 'der alten religion anhengig, geistlich oder weltlich' untroubled in their religion

§17: 'Doch sollen alle andere, so obgemelten beden religionen nit anhengig, in diesem frieden nit gemeint sondern genzlich ausgeschlossen sein' (the OCR runs 'bedenreligionennit' together and reads 'ssin'); the clause names no group

§18, headed by Mirbt '(Reservatum ecclesiasticum)': a churchman who leaves 'unser alten religion' gives up his see and its income at once, 'jedoch seinen eren onnachteilig'; the chapter may choose 'eine person der alten religion verwant'
§19, in Mirbt's summary only: church goods seized by the Protestant estates stay with them

§20: church jurisdiction not exercised against the Augsburg Confession's religion, ministries and ceremonies, and to 'ruhen, eingestelt und suspendirt sein' 'bis zu entlicher vergleichung der religion' (OCR 'entlieher')
§24: subjects of either religion may move 'mit iren weib und kindern', sell their goods against a fair release from serfdom and departure tax, 'unverhindert menniklichs', without loss of honor

§25: if agreement through general council, national assembly, colloquies or imperial negotiations fails, the peace still stands, 'ein bestendiger beharrlicher und unbedingter, für und für, ewig werender friet'
§106: the Kammergericht's judge and assessors may be presented 'von beyden der alten Religion und der Augspurgischen Confession'
Pallavicino's article: the concord holds also among the nobility directly subject to the emperor and in imperial cities where both religions had been in force, so that both live together peaceably
Sarpi: the Catholics would not let bishops or abbots change religion and keep their posts, nor let the cities that had received the Interim return to the Augsburg Confession

Sarpi: 'The Catholicks were content that the Cities should do as they pleased, and the Protestants gave over their pretence concerning the Ecclesiasticks' (long s normalized; 'the;Proteſtants', 'prerence' in OCR)
Pallavicino's article on oaths 'per Dio, e per l'Euangelio', so that Protestants are not forced 'à giurar pe' Santi'
Pallavicino's article: no estate may draw another's lord or subject to its religion, nor protect vassals against their lord
Pallavicino: Ferdinand declared that the temporal subjects of church princes were not bound, like lay princes' subjects, to keep the prince's religion or change country
Sarpi tells a declaration by Ferdinand after the recess concerning places subject to church princes; the passage breaks off in the OCR
Pallavicino: Ferdinand judged it best not to decide by which of the four proposed ways concord might be reached, and put it off to a future diet

Paul IV to Ferdinand, 18 Dec 1555: the popes had worked that the Augsburg assembly should break up with religion untouched rather than reach a recess 'tam perniciosum' (OCR 'perniciosura'), reached against his will, Ferdinand's and all Catholics'

Paul IV to Bishop Wolfgang of Passau, 18 Dec 1555: 'Nam quid alienius ab ea potuit deliberari [OCR 'dehberari'], quam quae in Augustae proximi conventus recessu decretum fuisse accepimus!' ('ea' is the Catholic faith of the sentence before)
Pallavicino: the pope 'fè perciò asprissime querele' with Ferdinand, set out by the nuncio Delfino, who returned from Rome early in 1556

Pallavicino: it seemed to Ferdinand that in the concessions harmful to Catholics plain necessity had kept him 'lungi da-' (OCR 'lungi da-*'; the next word is lost in the OCR), and that where the choice was his he had shown the greatest zeal (OCR 'telo'); he answered 'con maniere più risentite' than his mild nature usually allowed
Pallavicino: the pope's complaints were taken as reproaches because of his ill will toward the House of Austria
Pallavicino says Sarpi tells the wars of Paul IV and Philip 'senza dirne i veri principij'
Sarpi: 'The Fame was' that Cardinal Truchsess of Augsburg, 'displeased with the liberty granted to the Confessionists', moved the pope; what the pope said is partly on lost lines

Pallavicino: Ferdinand's and Bavaria's subjects asked not to be under a harder condition than their neighbors; they were answered that by the recesses vassals must 'seguir la Religion de' Padroni, ò à partirsi'

Pallavicino's verdict: the recess proved the more harmful in the long run the more helpful it seemed then; the Germans slept on this 'oppio', and it cost Germany in another age 'vn lunghissimo trauaglio, con tante stragi e desolazioni'

Duke Christoph of Württemberg's mandate punishes Anabaptists, Schwenckfelders and others in honor, body and goods, 'dann sie auch in jungstem zuo Augspurg ufgeriebtem [sic OCR] religionsfridenstand und Freistellung mit nichten begriffen, sonder darvon usgesohlossen [sic OCR]'
Bossert: the first draft dates from 1556, as the councillors' advice of 11 September 1556 shows; the printed copy carries Duke Christoph's additions; the draft was still debated early in 1557
'Zwinglischer' was written above the line in Duke Christoph's own hand (Bossert's note a)

The Erläuterung says that at Worms in 1557 each Lutheran party wished to be the true kin of the Augsburg Confession and to shut the others out of the Religious Peace; the Catholics answered they must first settle who those were
The Erläuterung was written by Schwenckfelder emigrants from Silesia; the host catalogue names Christopher Schultz; first printed at Jauer in 1771
Schaff: Frederick III 'was threatened with exclusion from the benefits of the Augsburg Treaty of Peace (concluded in 1555), since Zwinglianism and Calvinism were not yet tolerated on German soil'

Nadal, Canisius and Ledesma, 1566: reconfirming the peace did not prejudice Trent's dogmas; its conditions held 'nihil ... praeterquam permissionem, dissimulationem ecclesiasticae iurisdictionis, ac iuris etiam imperialis debiti suspensionem', yielding 'ad tempus' to hard necessity
The 1566 opinion: the Holy See 'ferre quidem dolenter' this, and does not approve all done in the recesses 'nec pacem hanc publice constitutam laudari'
The subscriptions of Nadal, Canisius and Ledesma on the 1566 opinion are autograph, by the editors' note

At Trent in 1563 the archbishop of Prague, for the emperor, said a draft seemed to overturn 'tutti i recessi delle diete alemanne in materie ecclesiastiche, e perciò rimetter le spade in mano alle parti pacificate'
Lützow: 'The Peace of Augsburg contained no reference to Bohemia, but it greatly encouraged the Lutheran party in that country'
The 1609 Letter of Majesty, quoted by the Bohemian estates in 1618, leaves them 'při tom pokoji, v svaté říši a náboženství, jenž Religionsfried slově, učiněném'
Westphalia: the 1555 peace 'rata habeatur sancteque et inviolabiliter servetur'
Westphalia gives its rights also to those 'qui inter illos reformati vocantur' (who among them are called Reformed)
Westphalia: 'Praeter religiones super nominatas nulla alia in sacro imperio Romano recipiatur vel toleretur'
Innocent X protested that 'Haereticis Augustanae, ut vocant, confessionis liberum suae haereseos exercitium' is allowed
Kriebel says the Schwenckfelders 'later were practically outlawed by the Augsburg Confession, by the Truce of Nuremberg, by the Treaty of Augsburg and by the Treaty of Westphalia'
Seipt: the Peace of Augsburg (1555) 'granted to every ruling prince the right to enforce his religion upon his subjects, and to banish all who refused to conform'
Schaeffer: 1555 was the year 'the signing of the articles of the Peace of Augsburg secured a temporary external repose for the Lutheran Church'
Pallavicino: Ferdinand consented to grave losses for the Catholic religion 'non però à perpetuo, mà fin' alla concordia finale'
Sarpi's summary: 'every one having Power to [estab]lish in his own State what Religion he will, and to forbid the other' (OCR 'liſh')
Sarpi: in the debate 'all inclined to the second proposition', to leave every one to his liberty, and it was resolved to let princes and states follow in their dominions what pleased them best
Salmerón, 1 Sept 1555: Ferdinand would lose his states, life and children rather than favor the heretics, and would permit nothing in the Diet against the faith or the Catholics
Nadal from Augsburg: 'non si fa niente della dieta, se non ch' guadagnano ogni giorno d' grosso li lutherani' (OCR 'deUa', 'U lutherani')
Canisius to Ignatius, 3 August 1555, quoted from Braunsberger: more harm than good is to be feared from the Diet, 'et nonest qui se opponat murum pro domo. Israél'
The Hutterite chronicle has a count tell arrested Brethren in 1557: 'denn die Konfession zu Augsburg hat es also beschlossen'; it may refer to the 1530 confession, and is not told as about the peace

contested_claims.claim: Whether the peace let rulers choose their subjects' religion
contested_claims.sides: The recess protects the estates' religion 'in iren fürstentumben, landen und herschaften' and gives subjects of both religions a right to leave: Mirbt's extract (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.16277-16279, 16316-16323) | Power 'to establish in his own State what Religion he will, and to forbid the other': Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.38458-38459) | A duty of vassals to 'seguir la Religion de' Padroni, ò à partirsi': Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.27527-27529) | 'the right to enforce his religion upon his subjects, and to banish all who refused': Seipt (seipt_schwenkfelder-hymnology_1909.txt l.2241-2243) | Exceptions held: the imperial cities (Pallavicino pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.27483-27486; Sarpi sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.38440-38442), church princes' subjects (Pallavicino pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.27505-27507), the churchmen's clause (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.16294-16298)

contested_claims.claim: Whether the peace was permanent or temporary
contested_claims.sides: Until final agreement and, failing that, 'ewig werender': the recess (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.16326-16332) | 'non però à perpetuo, mà fin' alla concordia finale': Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.27413-27415) | 'a temporary external repose for the Lutheran Church': Schaeffer (arndt_true-christianity_boehm-schaeffer1868.txt l.532-535) | a 'permissionem' yielding 'ad tempus': the 1566 Jesuits (nadal_epistolae-v3-lat_1902.txt l.5676-5681) | Pallavicino's own list of articles also gives the clause that the peace stays 'ferma ed inuiolabile' (OCR 'ferma cd inaiai abile') if no final concord comes (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.27479-27481)

contested_claims.claim: Whether the peace was the first legal toleration
contested_claims.sides: No held text says 'first' or 'toleration'; the recess says 'frieden' and 'fridstand' (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.16291, 16323) | Passau 1552 came before it: Westphalia (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.21625-21626), Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.27462-27464) | Kriebel names 'the Truce of Nuremberg' among earlier acts (kriebel_schwenkfelders-in-pennsylvania_1904.txt l.1089)

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Reformed (Calvinists) were left out by the 1555 recess
contested_claims.sides: The recess names no one; it excludes 'alle andere' (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.16290-16292) | Later texts put Zwinglians outside: Duke Christoph's mandate (taeuferakten-wuerttemberg_quellen-geschichte-wiedertaeufer-1-deu_bossert1930.txt l.9244, 9280, 9307-9311); Schaff on Frederick III (schaff_second-helvetic-confession-heidelberg-catechism_1919.txt l.1819-1821) | Westphalia gives the rights also to those 'qui inter illos reformati vocantur', among the Catholic and Augsburg Confession estates and subjects (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.21736-21742)

contested_claims.claim: Whether Ferdinand gave way or held firm
contested_claims.sides: He would permit nothing against the faith: Salmerón, 1 Sept 1555 (salmeron_epistolae-v2-lat_1906.txt l.8455-8461) | He 'consentì à grauissimi detrimenti della Religion Cattolica', and Ferdinand felt ('parendogli') the harmful concessions plainly necessary: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.27413, 27568-27574) | Cause: Charles's curt answer leaving it to Ferdinand, in Ferdinand's own defence as Pallavicino gives it (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.27419-27423); the debate where 'all inclined' to liberty, Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.38401-38404)

contested_claims.claim: Ferdinand's declaration on church princes' subjects: its terms and consent

claims.claim: The 1580 title page of the Ecclesiastical History names no author
The History was long credited to Beza; Reuss asks whether he wrote it and finds the tradition's foundations anything but solid
Reuss thought Beza did not compile the History himself but directed it closely and contributed his memories of the Colloquy of Poissy
Baum and Cunitz show the History's Poissy chapter copying La Place's Commentaires word for word in places
The History is a Reformed narrative, polemical in places, e.g. calling most prelates incapable of treating religion
Baum and Cunitz say Beza's speech of 9 September was probably first printed under his own care a few days after the colloquy
On 9 September, about noon, the court gathered in the great refectory of the nuns at Poissy
The king sat with Orleans and Navarre on his right, and the queen mother and the Queen of Navarre on his left
Three cardinals sat on each side of the hall, and below them thirty-six bishops and archbishops, with clergy and doctors behind
Sarpi gives six cardinals on 9 September. The OCR reads 'second of September'; the passage describes the session of 9 September
Pallavicino gives five cardinals besides the legate and forty bishops who had come for the Estates
The History says twelve ministers came with 22 deputies of the provincial churches, brought in by the Duke of Guise
Sarpi says the Protestant ministers were fourteen
The ministers stood bare-headed at the barrier, and Beza, chosen by the others, spoke
Beza wished that all might with one voice sing a hymn to the Lord and hold out hands to one another
Beza's printed speech: Christ's body is as far from the bread and wine as the highest heaven from the earth
The History's narrative: Christ's body, though truly offered and given in the Supper, was as far from the bread as heaven from earth
The prelates began to murmur; some said 'Blasphemavit', others rose to leave
Tournon asked the king and queen that Beza be silenced or allowed to withdraw
The History: the king did not stir, and Beza finished his speech
Sarpi: Beza spoke with such heat that he was commanded to conclude
Languet, in a note by Baum and Cunitz, says they let Beza finish
Catherine, on 14 September, says she nearly silenced Beza but held back; known through a note by Baum and Cunitz from Le Laboureur
Beza gave the confession of the Reformed churches to the king
Sarpi says Beza spoke after praying on his knee

After the first session the prelates resolved that Lorraine, helped by Despence, would answer on the Church and the Supper only. A counter-confession would follow, with condemnation for refusal. The History gives no date; dated 10 September by Baum and Cunitz from Vermigli's letter (HE1 l.29024-29027)
The second session was on 16 September in the same hall
Lorraine told the king he was the Church's son, not its lord; a member, not its head
The prelates' assembly received the Society of Jesus on Monday 15 September as a college, not a new order, on condition it take another title
The royal letters of 1562 call the Poissy meeting the 'assemblée du clergé et concile national'
The legate, Cardinal of Ferrara, came to court on 19 September, by Vermigli's Relatio in a note by Baum and Cunitz
The History says Lainez (called 'Lieva') was in the legate's train; the editors correct the name
Lainez's editors date his arrival at Paris on 17 September and at Saint-Germain on 19 September
On 24 September the History gives five cardinals, fifteen or sixteen doctors, some bishops, and twelve ministers only
Polanco dates the third meeting to Wednesday 24 September; his editors' note reads 24 September 1561
Polanco says on Friday 26 September the same five cardinals came, with 25 bishops, and the queen mother despite the rain
Polanco says Ferrara and Tournon would not attend these disputations
Martyr spoke in Italian on 26 September, at the queen's wish, Polanco says
Lainez spoke in Italian, always turning his speech to the queen, for about three quarters of an hour, Polanco says
Lainez: it is not for the queen, nor for temporal princes, to handle matters of faith; they belong to the pope and the general council
Lainez: with the general council open, such meetings were neither fitting nor lawful
Lainez's copy was begun by Codreto and finished by Polanco, with Lainez's own corrections, the editors say
Coudret says Polanco was present
Polanco's letter is printed from his own drafts, the editors say
The ministers' declaration of 26 September says they speak for a million people in France, Switzerland, Poland, Germany, England and Scotland
Lorraine produced a paper that proved a copy of a Württemberg preachers' confession of 1559
The History says Lorraine sent for Augsburg-confession ministers 'afin de les divifer'
The History says the third conference, the last, went without order or secretaries
At Catherine's order two bishops (Montluc, Du Val) and three doctors (Despence, Salignac, Boutelier) conferred with five ministers (Martyr, Beza, Des Gallars, Marlorat, L'Espine)
The conference met on 29 September; Baum and Cunitz correct the text's date
On 1 October the statement was recast at Despence's urging
The statement says Christ in the Supper truly gives the substance of his body and blood
The History says Lorraine said he had never believed otherwise; Des Gallars agrees, Beza's letter of 4 October is silent
The formula went to Poissy on 4 October and was rejected as captious on 9 October
The prelates' conclusion found the statement not only insufficient but captious, with errors
Unless Beza and his company at once confessed and signed the Catholic confession, they would not be heard again
The conclusion asks that they be barred from the realm under the king's penalty. There had been but one God, one king, one faith and one law
The Catholic confession says Christ's body and blood are present really and transubstantially under the species of bread and wine
The canons' preamble: the king summoned the prelates of the Gallican Church to Poissy, pending the general council
The canons submit all decrees to the pope
The first canon treats the naming and examination of bishops
The last canon tells the faithful to abhor Luther, Zwingli and Calvin as heresiarchs
The canons close 'Acta Poissiaci ... 1561. Pridie Idus Oct.', in Languet's Latin given by Baum and Cunitz
After 9 October the ministers could never obtain a debate on their confession, the History says
The prelates dismissed their doctors on 13 October and went home
The German theologians reached Paris on 19 October, Baum and Cunitz say
Catherine: the two meetings brought only confusion of disputes upon disputes, more discord than union

After Lorraine's reply, Catherine thought it good that the prelates enter a gracious colloquy with the ministers on their confession (the two meetings fit the sessions of 24 and 26 September, which Polanco dates)
Catherine's smaller conference of five or six did not please the other prelates
Catherine: nothing in the canons can remedy the troubles
Catherine will await the next general council, not knowing what to expect of it
Catherine's letter is dated at Saint-Germain, October 1561, signed CATERINE; the OCR of the day reads 'iS.'
The heading above Catherine's letter is Aymon's
Sarpi: the Pope was very glad the colloquy was dissolved without doing anything
Pallavicino: neither side surrendered, and each claimed a kind of victory
Pallavicino: French Catholics blamed the colloquy for the Huguenots' freedom to profess their faith openly
Pallavicino: no national council was agreed. Catholics thought it an insult to the general council; the Reformed knew French prelates would not grant them equal judging power
Bonnet: the colloquy everywhere increased the audacity of the Reformed
The Edict of January suspended penalties for Reformed meetings by day outside the towns. It did so until the general council decided or the king ordered otherwise
The Edict's reason: awaiting God's grace to reunite the subjects in one fold
The Edict also forbids preaching inside the towns, by day or night
Waterworth: the articles proposed at Poissy were secretly submitted to canonists at Trent in 1562, to be examined
Pallavicino reports Lorraine at Trent, 1563: the clergy and Estates gathered at Poissy were held back with great difficulty
A 1607 letter the diary's editor gives to James Melvill (the attribution in square brackets) cites the Colloquy of Poissy as a warning against colloquies
Melville's letter is in the 1607 continuation of his diary
Bersier: in 1872 the synod president opened a session with Beza's confession of sins first read at Poissy
The July assembly resolved again to call the prelates to Poissy. The ministers would have safe-conduct to be heard, to see whether they could be reunited to the Roman Church
Baum and Cunitz say that assembly's deliberations ran from 23 June to 11 July
The History says the assembly made the Edict of July
Bretagne, speaking for the Third Estate, asked the king to call a free and lawful national council and preside over it
A further list of requests at the Estates asks for a free and lawful national council, as already promised
L'Hospital, in the History's summary: the king granted a safe-conduct hoping a friendly conference would profit, so no one could say they were condemned unheard
The ministers asked that bishops not be their judges, being the other party, and that all be decided by the word of God alone
The king: 'je vous ay fait affembler'
Martyr and Beza were sent for by letters of the King of Navarre; Martyr from Zurich, Beza from Geneva
Des Gallars had been pastor of the London church for two years, the editors say
The History names fourteen ministers in all
Baum and Cunitz count La Tour as the twelfth minister and the lay deputies as 22
Polanco names the five cardinals of 24 September as Lorraine, Armagnac, Bourbon, Chatillon and Guise
The queen gave the ministers her word that the clergy would not be their judges, with the Admiral present
The title of one early edition of Beza's speech, listed by Baum and Cunitz, calls 9 September a Tuesday
The ministers' first petition is dated 17 August in the History
Languet wrote on 1 August that the bishops' assembly had begun three days before. Brulart gives 1 August; De Thou 10 August, which the editors reject
Polanco's 26 September formula reads 'substantialiter'; the History prints a French statement without it
Pallavicino is of the Society of Jesus (title)
Lainez is called general of the Society of Jesus by Pallavicino
Calvin advised Beza by letter, 10 and 24 September 1561
Crespin's notice nearly reproduces La Place's narrative, Benoît says
Beza was minister at Geneva then
Beza's printed speech: believers are made partakers of Christ's body and blood in a spiritual way and through faith, as truly as they see the sacraments
Sarpi was a Venetian friar of the Servite order
Pallavicino's history sets out to refute a false history published under the name Pietro Soave Polano (Sarpi) (title)
Sarpi writes against the papal power: the council confirmed the 'exorbitant power' of the See of Rome

contested_claims.claim: Who wrote the Ecclesiastical History
contested_claims.sides: Credited to Beza by long tradition and by the Library catalogue (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.2); the 1580 title page names no author (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.110-130) | Reuss: Beza directed it and gave his Poissy memories but did not compile it (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t3-fra_baum-cunitz-reuss1889.txt l.2002-2010) | Soldan and Heppe, cited by Reuss, deny Beza wrote it (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t3-fra_baum-cunitz-reuss1889.txt l.1629-1648)
contested_claims.note: The entry never calls the History Beza's; it prints his speech as participant words.
